screens.title: Command and Template Method
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore two complementary behavioral patterns that help you structure behavior in object-oriented systems: Command and Template Method. You'll learn how the Command pattern turns a request into a first-class object you can pass, queue, log, and even undo. You will also learn how the Template Method pattern fixes an algorithm's structure in a base class while letting subclasses implement specific steps. Both patterns improve extensibility and maintainability, but they do so in different ways: Command isolates requests and responsibilities, while Template Method centralizes control flow and delegates variation. A concrete example you will revisit is a smart-home remote that uses command objects to turn lights on and off and to support undo. For Template Method, we'll use a house-building template where the overall build sequence is fixed, yet concrete builders supply foundation, walls, and roof steps. By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose which pattern fits GUI actions, framework hooks, and undoable operations, and you will be able to implement both patterns in Java. Consider how your current projects handle requests and algorithm structure; are actions objects or direct method calls?

keyIdea.title: Two ways to manage behavior

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Command & Template
Command and Template Method
Two behavioral patterns that organize requests and algorithm structure to make code extensible and maintainable.
Orientation

The Command pattern wraps an operation as an object so you can store it, queue it, or reverse it later. The Template Method pattern defines a fixed step sequence and lets subclasses implement the variable steps. Together they help you choose between treating behavior as data versus treating steps as a controlled extension point.

In this lesson
Implement Command
Encapsulate actions for undo, queuing, and decoupled invocation.
Coming up
Template Method
Provide a template algorithm while deferring specific steps to subclasses.
Why it matters
Maintainability
Reduce coupling and centralize control flow for predictable extension points.
Concept Map
Command ↔ Receiver ↔ Invoker • Template Method → Base + Steps
Remote control example
Buttons send command objects to the TV. The TV executes commands without exposing implementation details.
House builder example
A base builder calls steps in order; concrete builders supply foundation, walls, and roof logic.
Quick takeaway
Choose Command when actions must be treated as objects. Choose Template Method when the sequence of steps is fixed but specific steps vary.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives guide the chapter and show what you will be able to do. First, you'll implement the Command pattern so you can encapsulate a request as an object and pass it around. This skill matters because it lets your application queue actions, store them for later execution, and wire undo behavior into a clear history. Second, you'll understand how Command supports undo and request queuing; you'll practice storing executed commands and reversing them to produce undo/redo. Third, you'll implement the Template Method pattern to define a fixed algorithm skeleton in a base class, while letting subclasses provide the variable steps. That helps you build frameworks where the general flow is controlled by the framework and specific behavior is supplied by application code. Finally, you'll learn to choose the right pattern for GUI actions or framework design, improving extensibility and maintainability in complex systems. Each objective includes hands-on practice and a verified competency milestone to validate your implementation.

screens.title: Command Pattern — What and why
screens.narratorSegment: The Command pattern turns an operation into an object that carries all the information needed to perform that operation. In practice this means you define a Command interface with an execute operation and often an undo operation. Concrete command classes hold a reference to the Receiver — the object that actually performs the work — and implement execute by delegating to the receiver with concrete parameters. This decouples the Invoker, which triggers commands, from the Receiver, which implements action logic. A concrete example is a smart-home remote control. The remote's button is an invoker that holds a TurnOnLight command. The command stores the target Light receiver and calls its turnOn method when executed. The same command object can be queued or stored in a history list so undo becomes possible by calling the command's undo method. A common misconception is to use Command for trivial single-method calls where no queuing, logging, or undo is needed; in these cases a direct method call is simpler. The key takeaway is that Command is most valuable when you must treat behavior as data: schedule it, persist it, or reverse it. How might you represent a macro in your application as a sequence of command objects?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Command encapsulates a request as an object so it can be parameterized, queued, logged, or undone.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Command Pattern
What the Command pattern does
Encapsulate requests as objects to decouple invokers from receivers.
Core participants
  • Command: declares execute and undo.
  • ConcreteCommand: binds a receiver and implements execute/undo.
  • Receiver: performs the actual work.
  • Invoker: asks a command to execute.
Example
A remote button uses a TurnOnLightCommand to call the living-room Light.turnOn method; the command also implements undo to call turnOff.
Common mistake
Applying Command to trivial single-method calls adds unnecessary complexity when no queuing, logging, or undo is required.
Pro tip
Keep commands small: store only the receiver and required parameters so undo can restore state without bloated objects.
Visualized flow
Invoker
Holds and triggers commands. Example: RemoteControl.pressButton()
Command
Encapsulates execute and undo. Example: TurnOnLightCommand
Receiver
Performs the real action. Example: Light.turnOn()
Key takeaway
Command turns behavior into data: schedule, persist, and reverse actions reliably while keeping invocation decoupled from implementation.

screens.title: Command Pattern Participants
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the participants of the Command pattern helps you distribute responsibilities correctly. The Command interface declares execute and often undo. ConcreteCommand implements these methods and holds a reference to the Receiver and any parameters needed. The Receiver knows how to perform the actual work — for example, a Light has turnOn and turnOff methods. The Invoker keeps a command reference and invokes execute when requested; it may also maintain a history to support undo. The Client creates ConcreteCommand instances, sets receivers, and configures invokers. A concrete walkthrough: the client creates a TurnOnLightCommand bound to a living-room Light. The client gives this command to the remote control invoker. When the user presses the button, the invoker calls execute and the receiver turns on the light. If you need undo, store the command in a history list when executed. A frequent misconception is confusing the Receiver with the Command; the receiver performs operations, the command just calls it. Ask yourself: which component in your design currently does the work, and which could become a command wrapper to enable undo or queuing? Command Pattern Participants means client creates commands, invoker triggers them, command delegates to receiver; history enables undo.. In practical terms, roles and responsibilities: command, concretecommand, receiver, invoker, client. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Pattern Participants
Participants and responsibilities
Map each role to concrete code and state you must store for undo or queuing.
Command (interface)
Declares execute() and undo() when undo is required.
ConcreteCommand
Stores receiver reference and any parameters. Implements execute/undo by delegating to the receiver.
Receiver
Performs the real operation, e.g., Light.turnOn()
Invoker
Triggers command execution and may maintain history for undo/redo.
Example flow
Client wires TurnOnLightCommand with a Light, sets it on the RemoteControl invoker, the user presses a button, the invoker calls execute, and the receiver turns on the light. The invoker can push the command to history for undo.
Example: minimal state for undo
A TurnOff command may store prior state or rely on the receiver's symmetric action in undo. For editors, store the exact text you removed so undo can re-insert it precisely.
Key Takeaway

Separate concerns: let commands represent intent, let receivers perform work, and let invokers manage execution and history.

screens.title: Command Example: SmartHomeApp
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the SmartHomeApp example to see Command in action. The Command interface declares execute() and undo() so concrete commands can perform and reverse actions. The Light receiver exposes turnOn and turnOff. TurnOnLightCommand holds a reference to the Light and implements execute by calling turnOn and undo by calling turnOff. The RemoteControl invoker stores the current command and a history list. When pressButton is called the invoker executes the command and pushes it onto history. When pressUndo is called the invoker pops the last command and calls undo. This example shows how a simple history makes undo straightforward for symmetric operations like turning lights on and off. A subtle point: not all actions have an obvious inverse; for those you must either store previous state in the command or implement compensating actions. Also notice where decoupling helps: the RemoteControl never needs to know about Light methods or details. Practice tracing the code while imagining more complex receivers like a media player or editor; the pattern scales the same way. keyIdea.title: Execute & Undo
keyIdea.text: Commands implement execute and undo; invokers run commands and keep history for undo/redo.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › SmartHomeApp Walkthrough
SmartHomeApp (Java)
A compact example demonstrating execute and undo with a remote and light.
interface Command {
  void execute();
  void undo();
}

class Light {
  public void turnOn() { System.out.println("Light is ON"); }
  public void turnOff() { System.out.println("Light is OFF"); }
}

class TurnOnLightCommand implements Command {
  private Light light;
  public TurnOnLightCommand(Light light) { this.light = light; }
  @Override public void execute() { light.turnOn(); }
  @Override public void undo() { light.turnOff(); }
}

class RemoteControl {
  private Command command;
  private List history = new ArrayList<>();
  public void setCommand(Command c) { command = c; }
  public void pressButton() { if (command!=null) { command.execute(); history.add(command); } }
  public void pressUndo() { if (!history.isEmpty()) { Command last = history.remove(history.size()-1); last.undo(); } }
}
Design note
When undo requires restoring arbitrary prior state, commands should capture that state at construction or before execute runs.
Concrete example output
The console prints Light is ON when execute is invoked and Light is OFF when undo is invoked, clearly tracing execute and undo behavior.
Key Takeaway

Commands make it easy to log and reverse operations; ensure commands have the state they need for reliable undo.

screens.title: Undo, Redo and Queuing with Command
screens.narratorSegment: Command naturally supports undo and redo because commands are objects you can store and replay. A common pattern is to push executed commands onto a history stack. To undo, pop the last command and call its undo method. For redo, keep an auxiliary stack of undone commands; re-executing a command pushes it back onto the main history. For queuing or asynchronous execution, commands can be placed into a queue and processed by a worker thread; this decouples request submission from execution time. The key implementation detail is that commands must carry sufficient information to reverse or reapply effects. For example, an InsertCommand in a text editor should capture the inserted string and its insertion index so undo can delete the exact substring. A misconception to avoid is assuming undo is automatic; only symmetric operations are trivially undoable. When operations are not symmetric, commands must record prior state snapshots or compensating actions. Consider performance and memory: storing full snapshots for every command may be expensive, so choose minimal state and consider coalescing related commands when appropriate. How would you design undo for batch edits in a real editor?

keyIdea.title: Undo/Redo basics
keyIdea.text: Use a history stack for undo, an undone stack for redo, and queues for asynchronous execution; ensure commands record needed state.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Undo & Queuing
Undo, redo and queuing
Patterns for managing command execution history and asynchronous requests.
Undo stack
Push executed commands onto a stack. Pop and call undo to reverse the last action.
Redo stack
When undoing, move the command to a redo stack. Re-execute to redo and push back to undo stack.
Queued execution
Place commands in a queue processed by a worker to decouple submission from execution time.
Concrete example
InsertCommand stores the inserted text and index so undo can delete those exact characters. DeleteCommand stores deleted text so undo can re-insert it verbatim.
Caveat

Not all operations are cheap to snapshot. Prefer storing minimal state or implementing compensating actions instead of full data copies when possible.

Key Takeaway

Design command objects to capture only what’s necessary to undo or redo, and use stacks/queues to manage execution and reversal.

screens.title: Template Method Pattern — What and why
screens.narratorSegment: The Template Method pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class and allows subclasses to override specific steps. The base class provides a final template method that calls a sequence of primitive operations and optional hook methods. Primitive operations are abstract and must be implemented by concrete subclasses; hook methods provide default behavior that subclasses can override when needed. A clear example from the chapter is a HouseBuilder abstract class with a final buildHouse method that calls layFoundation, buildWalls, installRoof, and addInterior. Concrete builders such as WoodenHouseBuilder and BrickHouseBuilder implement the primitive operations and optionally override the hook to customize interior work. The pattern matters in framework design because it centralizes the control flow while exposing safe extension points. A common mistake is making too many steps abstract, which shifts too much responsibility to subclasses and weakens the template's control. Balance fixed steps with extension points so the base class retains meaningful supervision of the algorithm. Template Method Pattern — What and why means template method fixes the algorithm structure and delegates variable steps to subclasses via abstract and hook methods.. In practical terms, define an algorithm skeleton and defer specific steps to subclasses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Template Method fixes the algorithm structure and delegates variable steps to subclasses via abstract and hook methods.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Template Method
What the Template Method does
Provide a final template method that defines step order and calls abstract/hook methods for customization.
Key elements
  • Template method: final, defines the algorithm sequence.
  • Primitive operations: abstract, must be implemented by subclasses.
  • Hook methods: optional default implementations that can be overridden.
Example: BuildHouse calls layFoundation, buildWalls, installRoof, addInterior; wooden and brick builders implement their specific steps.
Common mistake
Making too many steps abstract so the base class loses control. Keep the template meaningful by leaving core structure in the base class.
House builder example
The abstract HouseBuilder defines buildHouse as final and declares primitive methods for foundation, walls, and roof. Concrete builders implement those primitives and may override addInterior as a hook.
Key Takeaway

Template Method centralizes the algorithm and provides safe, tested extension points via abstract and hook methods.

screens.title: Template Method Participants
screens.narratorSegment: Template Method introduces a small set of participants that together enforce an algorithm structure while permitting variation. The abstract class defines the final template method, which sequences calls to primitive operations and hook methods. Primitive operations are abstract methods that concrete subclasses must implement — these are the variation points. Hook methods provide optional extension points with default behavior. Concrete subclasses implement primitives and may override hooks to customize nonessential behavior. For example, the HouseBuilder abstract class implements buildHouse and calls layFoundation, buildWalls, installRoof, and addInterior. WoodenHouseBuilder implements the primitives and overrides addInterior to provide a rustic interior. An important design decision is which steps to make primitive and which to supply as hooks; too many primitives reduce control, and too few reduce flexibility. Think of the base class as the conductor: it decides the tempo and order, and subclasses play the instruments. This leads to predictable extension in frameworks where the framework must remain in control while allowing application code to vary behavior. Template Method Participants means the abstract class controls flow via the template method and delegates variable behavior to primitive and hook methods implemented by subclasses.. In practical terms, abstract class, template method, primitive operations, and hooks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Template Anatomy
Roles inside Template Method
Map of the abstract class and the extension points subclasses implement.
Core elements
  1. Template method: final sequence of steps.
  2. Primitive operations: abstract methods for concrete behavior.
  3. Hook methods: optional defaults that can be overridden.
Decide which operations must remain in control and which can be delegated. Too many abstract methods and the template becomes just a wrapper; too few and subclasses cannot customize needed behavior.
Concrete builder examples
WoodenHouseBuilder implements primitive methods to lay a wooden foundation, wooden walls, and wooden roof. BrickHouseBuilder implements concrete steps for concrete foundation and brick walls while using the default interior hook.
Key Takeaway

Choose primitive operations for essential variation and hooks for optional tweaks so subclasses have enough control without breaking the algorithm.

screens.title: Template Method Example: HouseBuilder
screens.narratorSegment: Let's step through the HouseBuilder example to see Template Method in code. The abstract HouseBuilder defines a final buildHouse method that sequences the steps: layFoundation, buildWalls, installRoof, addInterior, and then prints a completion message. Primitive operations layFoundation, buildWalls, and installRoof are protected and abstract, so concrete builders must implement them. addInterior is a hook with a default implementation; subclasses may override it. WoodenHouseBuilder implements the three primitives with wooden-specific messages and overrides addInterior to provide a rustic interior. BrickHouseBuilder implements the primitives for concrete foundation and brick walls and uses the default interior hook. This design shows how the template method enforces order and ensures the algorithm always runs the same sequence, while subclasses supply the necessary details. A common misconception is that Template Method prevents any variation; in fact it provides controlled variation. Think about framework scenarios where the framework must guarantee order and safety while letting application code inject domain-specific behavior. Template Method Example: HouseBuilder means a final template method defines the fixed sequence; concrete subclasses implement primitive methods and optionally override hooks.. In practical terms, walkthrough of the abstract template method and concrete builders. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: A final template method defines the fixed sequence; concrete subclasses implement primitive methods and optionally override hooks.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › HouseBuilder Walkthrough
HouseBuilder template in Java
Abstract class defines the final template method and primitive/hook methods.
abstract class HouseBuilder {
  public final void buildHouse() {
    layFoundation();
    buildWalls();
    installRoof();
    addInterior();
    System.out.println("House built successfully!");
  }

  protected abstract void layFoundation();
  protected abstract void buildWalls();
  protected abstract void installRoof();

  protected void addInterior() { System.out.println("Adding basic interior (default)."); }
}

class WoodenHouseBuilder extends HouseBuilder {
  @Override protected void layFoundation() { System.out.println("Laying wooden foundation."); }
  @Override protected void buildWalls() { System.out.println("Building wooden walls."); }
  @Override protected void installRoof() { System.out.println("Installing wooden roof."); }
  @Override protected void addInterior() { System.out.println("Adding rustic wooden interior."); }
}
Design note
Mark the template method as final to prevent subclasses from changing the overall algorithm order and to keep the structure reliable.
Misconception

Template Method is not a one-size-fits-all solution. Avoid putting too much variability into primitives that break invariants the base class expects.

Key Takeaway

Use Template Method for reliable algorithm structure and controlled extension in frameworks and domain services.

screens.title: When to choose Command vs Template Method
screens.narratorSegment: Picking the right pattern depends on what you need to control. Choose the Command pattern when you need to treat actions as data: schedule them, persist them, combine them into macros, or reverse them with undo. Typical use cases include menu actions in GUIs, macro recording, and queued tasks. The Template Method is the right fit when an algorithm must follow a fixed sequence but parts of that sequence require domain-specific implementations — common in frameworks and pipelines. A helpful contrast: Command focuses on who performs an action at runtime and how to manage that action, while Template Method focuses on the order of steps in an algorithm and where to insert custom behavior. A common misconception is to try to use Template Method to implement undoable actions or to use Command to enforce algorithmic sequence — each pattern addresses different concerns. For real systems you may use both: a framework may use Template Method to define a pipeline, while individual steps inside that pipeline are implemented as Commands for queuing or undo. Ask yourself whether you need to treat behavior as persistent data or to provide disciplined extension points.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Pattern Comparison
Command vs Template Method
Side-by-side concerns to guide pattern selection.
Command
  • Treats operations as objects you can queue, store, and undo.
  • Decouples invoker from receiver implementation.
  • Good for GUI actions, macro recording, and asynchronous tasks.
Template Method
  • Fixes algorithm sequence in a base class and delegates steps to subclasses.
  • Common in frameworks where order and invariants must be preserved.
  • Use hooks for optional customization without breaking the flow.
Combined use
You can combine patterns: a Template Method pipeline can call Commands as step implementations, giving you both disciplined order and behavior-as-data advantages.
Key Takeaway

Match pattern intent to system needs: data-driven actions use Command; fixed-algorithm frameworks use Template Method.

screens.title: Activity 1: Text Editor Command History
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity asks you to implement a simple text editor using the Command pattern. The provided starter code includes a TextEditor receiver with insertText and deleteText methods and a command interface. Your tasks are to implement InsertCommand and DeleteCommand so they execute the action and can undo it reliably. InsertCommand should store the inserted text and the insertion point so undo can remove the exact characters. DeleteCommand should capture deleted text before removing it so undo can reinsert it. Use an EditorInvoker with a history stack to manage execution and undo. When testing, run a sequence of insert and delete commands, then undo them step by step and observe the editor's content restoring to previous states. Pay attention to edge cases such as deleting more characters than exist and undo after multiple operations. This exercise reinforces designing command objects that carry the minimal state required to reverse effects, and it practices wiring clients, invokers, and receivers together cleanly. Text Editor Command History
Implement InsertCommand and DeleteCommand so each can be executed and undone reliably.
// Command Interface
interface EditorCommand {
  void execute();
  void undo();
}

// Receiver
class TextEditor {
  private StringBuilder text = new StringBuilder();
  public void insertText(String newText) { /* appends text */ }
  public void deleteText(int length) { /* deletes suffix */ }
}

// TODO: Implement InsertCommand and DeleteCommand to capture minimal state
Testing tips
Run sequences of inserts and deletes, then undo step-by-step. Test edge cases and ensure delete stores deleted text for undo.
Pro tip

When undoing, avoid reaching into receiver internals; commands should instruct the receiver to restore or apply state via its public API.

Key Takeaway

Commands must capture sufficient state to undo reliably; the invoker manages history and orchestrates undo/redo.

screens.title: Activity 2: Data Processing Pipeline with Template Method
screens.narratorSegment: This activity asks you to implement a DataProcessor abstract class that defines the processData template method and primitive and hook operations for concrete data processors. The template should call readData, transformData, validateData, and writeData in sequence. Make readData, transformData, and writeData abstract, and implement validateData as a hook with a default returning true. Implement CSVDataProcessor and XMLDataProcessor as concrete subclasses. In CSVDataProcessor override validateData to perform CSV-specific checks and optionally simulate a failure path. Run both processors to observe the template method enforcing the order and the hook affecting whether writeData runs. This exercise demonstrates how Template Method centralizes control flow while allowing concrete classes to supply domain logic. A key misconception is assuming validateData must be abstract; making it a hook lets most subclasses use the default behavior while still giving the option to override. Think about pipeline concerns like error handling and logging: keep those in the base template so every concrete processor benefits from consistent lifecycle behavior. Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Activity: Data Pipeline
DataProcessor Template
Create an abstract template and supply CSV and XML concrete processors.
abstract class DataProcessor {
  public final void processData() {
    readData();
    transformData();
    if (validateData()) writeData();
  }
  protected abstract void readData();
  protected abstract void transformData();
  protected abstract void writeData();
  protected boolean validateData() { return true; }
}

class CSVDataProcessor extends DataProcessor { /* implement primitives and override validateData */ }
Testing tips
Run processors with valid and invalid simulated data to confirm the hook prevents write when validation fails and that the template sequence remains fixed.
Pro tip

Keep lifecycle concerns like logging and error handling inside the template method so all subclasses inherit consistent behavior.

Key Takeaway

Template Method enforces a consistent pipeline while letting concrete classes implement domain-specific steps and optional validation.

screens.title: Assessment Questions and Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Let's review the assessment questions and the common mistakes to watch for. One assessment asks which pattern suits a graphics editor that needs undo/redo for drawing operations; the correct answer is Command because it encapsulates each drawing action as an object you can store and reverse. Common mistakes include overusing Command for trivial calls where no reuse, queuing, or undo is needed, and making too many template steps abstract so the base class loses meaningful control. When designing, evaluate whether behavior should be treated as data or whether you need a fixed algorithm skeleton. Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Assessment Review
Assessment review and pitfalls
Two checkpoint questions and common mistakes summarized.
Question 1
Which pattern fits a graphics editor with undo for drawing operations? Answer: Command — encapsulate drawing actions as objects and store them in history.
Question 2
Which pattern fits an online quiz flow where load, present, score, and display are fixed but presentation and scoring vary? Answer: Template Method — a base quiz class defines the sequence and concrete quizzes implement presentation and scoring.
Top mistakes
  • Using Command for simple direct calls with no queuing or undo.
  • Making too many template methods abstract and losing base-class control.
  • Not capturing enough state in commands to perform reliable undo.
Final takeaway

Match the pattern to the problem: behavior-as-data choose Command; fixed algorithm skeleton choose Template Method. Avoid over-engineering.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Keep these three concise concepts in mind as you apply the patterns. First, the Command pattern encapsulates requests as objects so invokers can queue, log, and undo operations while remaining decoupled from the receiver. Second, the Template Method pattern defines a final algorithm skeleton in a base class and delegates specific steps to subclasses via primitive and optional hook methods; this is ideal for frameworks and pipelines. Third, pattern selection matters: use Command when behavior must be manipulated as data, and use Template Method when you must guarantee step order while allowing controlled variations. Each concept points to a design tradeoff: flexibility versus control, behavior-as-data versus controlled extension. Ask yourself which tradeoff your feature requires before you pick a pattern. Module 8 › Chapter 8.7 › Quick Reference
Commands: structure
Use an interface for execute/undo; keep command objects minimal and focused on state needed for reversal.
Template: structure
Mark the template method final and keep primitive methods for subclasses to implement required steps.
Design tradeoff

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore two complementary behavioral patterns that help you structure behavior in object-oriented systems: Command and Template Method. You'll learn how the Command pattern turns a request into a first-class object you can pass, queue, log, and even undo. You will also learn how the Template Method pattern fixes an algorithm's structure in a base class while letting subclasses implement specific steps. Both patterns improve extensibility and maintainability, but they do so in different ways: Command isolates requests and responsibilities, while Template Method centralizes control flow and delegates variation. A concrete example you will revisit is a smart-home remote that uses command objects to turn lights on and off and to support undo. For Template Method, we'll use a house-building template where the overall build sequence is fixed, yet concrete builders supply foundation, walls, and roof steps. By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose which pattern fits GUI actions, framework hooks, and undoable operations, and you will be able to implement both patterns in Java. Consider how your current projects handle requests and algorithm structure; are actions objects or direct method calls?

These learning objectives guide the chapter and show what you will be able to do. First, you'll implement the Command pattern so you can encapsulate a request as an object and pass it around. This skill matters because it lets your application queue actions, store them for later execution, and wire undo behavior into a clear history. Second, you'll understand how Command supports undo and request queuing; you'll practice storing executed commands and reversing them to produce undo/redo. Third, you'll implement the Template Method pattern to define a fixed algorithm skeleton in a base class, while letting subclasses provide the variable steps. That helps you build frameworks where the general flow is controlled by the framework and specific behavior is supplied by application code. Finally, you'll learn to choose the right pattern for GUI actions or framework design, improving extensibility and maintainability in complex systems. Each objective includes hands-on practice and a verified competency milestone to validate your implementation.

Beyond implementation, this chapter includes hands-on activities and assessment items to validate your understanding. You'll implement a text-editor command history that supports insert and delete commands with undo. That task tests your ability to encapsulate state inside command objects and restore it on undo. You'll also implement a data processing pipeline using Template Method where read, transform, and write steps are implemented by concrete subclasses while validation remains a hook. These exercises emphasize practical A P I design, correct separation of responsibilities, and clear client code that uses invokers or base classes. The provided assessment questions ask you to pick which pattern fits a graphics editor with undo and which pattern fits a quiz flow where steps are fixed but implementations vary. Completing the milestones proves you can both code and reason about tradeoffs in real applications.

The Command pattern turns an operation into an object that carries all the information needed to perform that operation. In practice this means you define a Command interface with an execute operation and often an undo operation. Concrete command classes hold a reference to the Receiver — the object that actually performs the work — and implement execute by delegating to the receiver with concrete parameters. This decouples the Invoker, which triggers commands, from the Receiver, which implements action logic. A concrete example is a smart-home remote control. The remote's button is an invoker that holds a TurnOnLight command. The command stores the target Light receiver and calls its turnOn method when executed. The same command object can be queued or stored in a history list so undo becomes possible by calling the command's undo method. A common misconception is to use Command for trivial single-method calls where no queuing, logging, or undo is needed; in these cases a direct method call is simpler. The key takeaway is that Command is most valuable when you must treat behavior as data: schedule it, persist it, or reverse it. How might you represent a macro in your application as a sequence of command objects?

Understanding the participants of the Command pattern helps you distribute responsibilities correctly. The Command interface declares execute and often undo. ConcreteCommand implements these methods and holds a reference to the Receiver and any parameters needed. The Receiver knows how to perform the actual work — for example, a Light has turnOn and turnOff methods. The Invoker keeps a command reference and invokes execute when requested; it may also maintain a history to support undo. The Client creates ConcreteCommand instances, sets receivers, and configures invokers. A concrete walkthrough: the client creates a TurnOnLightCommand bound to a living-room Light. The client gives this command to the remote control invoker. When the user presses the button, the invoker calls execute and the receiver turns on the light. If you need undo, store the command in a history list when executed. A frequent misconception is confusing the Receiver with the Command; the receiver performs operations, the command just calls it. Ask yourself: which component in your design currently does the work, and which could become a command wrapper to enable undo or queuing? Command Pattern Participants means client creates commands, invoker triggers them, command delegates to receiver; history enables undo.. In practical terms, roles and responsibilities: command, concretecommand, receiver, invoker, client. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the SmartHomeApp example to see Command in action. The Command interface declares execute() and undo() so concrete commands can perform and reverse actions. The Light receiver exposes turnOn and turnOff. TurnOnLightCommand holds a reference to the Light and implements execute by calling turnOn and undo by calling turnOff. The RemoteControl invoker stores the current command and a history list. When pressButton is called the invoker executes the command and pushes it onto history. When pressUndo is called the invoker pops the last command and calls undo. This example shows how a simple history makes undo straightforward for symmetric operations like turning lights on and off. A subtle point: not all actions have an obvious inverse; for those you must either store previous state in the command or implement compensating actions. Also notice where decoupling helps: the RemoteControl never needs to know about Light methods or details. Practice tracing the code while imagining more complex receivers like a media player or editor; the pattern scales the same way. Command Example: SmartHomeApp means commands implement execute and undo; invokers run commands and keep history for undo/redo.. In practical terms, step through the java example that shows execute and undo. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Command naturally supports undo and redo because commands are objects you can store and replay. A common pattern is to push executed commands onto a history stack. To undo, pop the last command and call its undo method. For redo, keep an auxiliary stack of undone commands; re-executing a command pushes it back onto the main history. For queuing or asynchronous execution, commands can be placed into a queue and processed by a worker thread; this decouples request submission from execution time. The key implementation detail is that commands must carry sufficient information to reverse or reapply effects. For example, an InsertCommand in a text editor should capture the inserted string and its insertion index so undo can delete the exact substring. A misconception to avoid is assuming undo is automatic; only symmetric operations are trivially undoable. When operations are not symmetric, commands must record prior state snapshots or compensating actions. Consider performance and memory: storing full snapshots for every command may be expensive, so choose minimal state and consider coalescing related commands when appropriate. How would you design undo for batch edits in a real editor?

The Template Method pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class and allows subclasses to override specific steps. The base class provides a final template method that calls a sequence of primitive operations and optional hook methods. Primitive operations are abstract and must be implemented by concrete subclasses; hook methods provide default behavior that subclasses can override when needed. A clear example from the chapter is a HouseBuilder abstract class with a final buildHouse method that calls layFoundation, buildWalls, installRoof, and addInterior. Concrete builders such as WoodenHouseBuilder and BrickHouseBuilder implement the primitive operations and optionally override the hook to customize interior work. The pattern matters in framework design because it centralizes the control flow while exposing safe extension points. A common mistake is making too many steps abstract, which shifts too much responsibility to subclasses and weakens the template's control. Balance fixed steps with extension points so the base class retains meaningful supervision of the algorithm. Template Method introduces a small set of participants that together enforce an algorithm structure while permitting variation. The abstract class defines the final template method, which sequences calls to primitive operations and hook methods. Primitive operations are abstract methods that concrete subclasses must implement — these are the variation points. Hook methods provide optional extension points with default behavior. Concrete subclasses implement primitives and may override hooks to customize nonessential behavior. For example, the HouseBuilder abstract class implements buildHouse and calls layFoundation, buildWalls, installRoof, and addInterior. WoodenHouseBuilder implements the primitives and overrides addInterior to provide a rustic interior. An important design decision is which steps to make primitive and which to supply as hooks; too many primitives reduce control, and too few reduce flexibility. Think of the base class as the conductor: it decides the tempo and order, and subclasses play the instruments. This leads to predictable extension in frameworks where the framework must remain in control while allowing application code to vary behavior. Picking the right pattern depends on what you need to control. Choose the Command pattern when you need to treat actions as data: schedule them, persist them, combine them into macros, or reverse them with undo. Typical use cases include menu actions in GUIs, macro recording, and queued tasks. The Template Method is the right fit when an algorithm must follow a fixed sequence but parts of that sequence require domain-specific implementations — common in frameworks and pipelines. A helpful contrast: Command focuses on who performs an action at runtime and how to manage that action, while Template Method focuses on the order of steps in an algorithm and where to insert custom behavior. A common misconception is to try to use Template Method to implement undoable actions or to use Command to enforce algorithmic sequence — each pattern addresses different concerns. For real systems you may use both: a framework may use Template Method to define a pipeline, while individual steps inside that pipeline are implemented as Commands for queuing or undo. Ask yourself whether you need to treat behavior as persistent data or to provide disciplined extension points.

Keep these three concise concepts in mind as you apply the patterns. First, the Command pattern encapsulates requests as objects so invokers can queue, log, and undo operations while remaining decoupled from the receiver. Second, the Template Method pattern defines a final algorithm skeleton in a base class and delegates specific steps to subclasses via primitive and optional hook methods; this is ideal for frameworks and pipelines. Third, pattern selection matters: use Command when behavior must be manipulated as data, and use Template Method when you must guarantee step order while allowing controlled variations. Each concept points to a design tradeoff: flexibility versus control, behavior-as-data versus controlled extension. Ask yourself which tradeoff your feature requires before you pick a pattern.
